title: Thorax, Pleura, Lungs, and Mediastinum
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter places the lungs, pleura, and mediastinal structures in the chest so that clinical findings can be traced to anatomy. It covers the surface projections of the lungs and pleura, the lobes and segments of each lung, the arrangement of structures at each hilum, the compartments of the mediastinum and the masses that arise in them, the innervation of the pleura, the openings and nerve supply of the diaphragm, and the course of the thoracic duct. Board questions use this anatomy to choose a needle site, predict where aspirated material settles, localize a mediastinal mass, explain shoulder pain, and recognize chylothorax.
prerequisites: Ribs, intercostal muscles, and the layers of the thoracic wall
Components of a typical spinal nerve and the dermatome map

Lymphatic drainage and chylomicron formation in the small intestine

connections.how: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch beside the left hilum, so a hilar or aortopulmonary mass can cause hoarseness.

connections.to: Pulmonary blood flow and ventilation (PU-5, PU-6)
connections.how: The hilar vessels carry the pulmonary and bronchial circulations, and negative pleural pressure links the chest wall to lung expansion.
Pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and chylothorax are read through the pleural borders, recesses, and thoracic duct described here.
Thymoma in the anterior mediastinum is linked to myasthenia gravis and other autoimmune disorders through faulty T cell selection.
The esophageal hiatus contributes to the antireflux barrier, and dietary fat absorbed as chylomicrons is what makes chyle milky.

terms.def: The lowest gutter of the pleural cavity, between costal and diaphragmatic pleura, which the lung does not fill in quiet breathing.
The groove on the inner lower border of each rib that shelters the intercostal vein, artery, and nerve.
The pyramidal portion of lung supplied by one segmental (tertiary) bronchus and segmental artery, surgically separable from its neighbors.
The tongue-shaped inferior part of the left upper lobe, the counterpart of the right middle lobe.
The depression on the medial surface of the lung where the root structures (bronchus, vessels, nerves, lymphatics) enter and leave.
The central compartment of the thoracic cavity between the two pleural sacs, from the thoracic inlet to the diaphragm.
The joint between manubrium and sternal body at the level of the second costal cartilage, marking the T4 to T5 plane.
The pleura lining the chest wall, diaphragm, and mediastinum, supplied by somatic nerves and sensitive to pain.
The pleura covering the lung surface, supplied by autonomic nerves and insensitive to sharp pain.
Pain perceived at a site distant from its source because both sites send afferents to the same spinal cord segments.
The dilated sac at the start of the thoracic duct, near L1 to L2, that collects lymph from the abdomen, pelvis, and lower limbs.
Accumulation of chyle, lymph rich in chylomicron triglyceride, in the pleural cavity after thoracic duct leak or obstruction.

sections.title: Surface projections of the lungs and pleura and the thoracentesis approach

blocks.text: Each lung sits inside a pleural sac that is larger than the lung itself. The parietal pleura lines the chest wall, diaphragm, and mediastinum; the visceral pleura covers the lung; and between them lies the pleural cavity, a potential space holding only a few milliliters of fluid. During quiet breathing the lower edge of the lung stays well above the lower edge of the sac, so both borders must be known to place a needle or interpret an effusion.

At the apex, the cervical pleura and lung rise about 2 to 3 cm above the medial third of the clavicle into the root of the neck, which is why a stab wound or needle at the base of the neck can cause pneumothorax. Anteriorly the two pleural sacs meet behind the sternum, but the left diverges at the fourth costal cartilage around the heart. Inferiorly, the borders are best remembered at three vertical lines, with the pleura two ribs lower than the lung at each line.

blocks.title: Lower borders of the lung and pleura
blocks.caption: The space between the two borders is the costodiaphragmatic recess, which the lung enters only on deep inspiration.

blocks.text: The costodiaphragmatic recess is the lowest part of the pleural cavity in an upright person, so free fluid collects there first and blunts the costophrenic angle on a radiograph. Because the posterior pleural border reaches rib 12 and even passes below it beside the vertebral column, a posterior approach to the kidney or a renal biopsy can open the pleural cavity.
The intercostal space and the needle path

The main intercostal vein, artery, and nerve run in the costal groove on the inner lower border of each rib, in that order from above down, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. The nerve is lowest and least protected by the groove. Small collateral branches run along the upper border of the rib below. A thoracentesis needle is therefore passed just above the upper border of the lower rib, high enough to miss the collateral branches, rather than below the rib above, where the main bundle lies.

blocks.title: Layers crossed by a thoracentesis needle
steps: Skin and subcutaneous tissue
Serratus anterior or latissimus dorsi, depending on site
External, internal, and innermost intercostal muscles
Endothoracic fascia
Costal parietal pleura (pain-sensitive)
Pleural cavity and costodiaphragmatic recess
blocks.caption: The needle crosses the space close to the upper border of the rib below, away from the costal groove of the rib above.

blocks.text: Moore describes entry through the ninth intercostal space in the midaxillary line during expiration, with the needle angled upward. Expiration raises the lung edge out of the recess, and the upward angle keeps the tip from passing through the diaphragm into the liver or spleen, which lie just beneath the floor of the recess.

blocks.title: Choosing a safe level
blocks.text: An upright patient has a moderate right effusion. At the midaxillary line the lung edge lies at rib 8 and the pleura at rib 10, so the recess spans the eighth and ninth intercostal spaces. A needle in the ninth space during expiration enters fluid below the lung. Entering the tenth space would pass below the pleural reflection, through the diaphragm and into the liver. Within the ninth space, the needle hugs the top of rib 10: hugging the bottom of rib 9 would strike the intercostal vein, artery, and nerve in its costal groove.

sections.title: Lobes and fissures of the two lungs and the anatomy of aspiration

blocks.text: The two lungs differ because of their neighbors. The heart bulges to the left, so the left lung is narrower and has a cardiac notch on its anterior border; the right dome of the diaphragm sits higher over the liver, so the right lung is shorter but wider and heavier. Each lobe is divided into bronchopulmonary segments, each supplied by one segmental bronchus and accompanying artery, which lets disease, and resection, be localized to a segment.

blocks.title: Right versus left lung
blocks.caption: The lingula is the left counterpart of the right middle lobe.

blocks.text: The oblique fissure runs from about the level of the T2 spinous process behind, around the side, to the sixth costal cartilage in front, roughly following rib 6. The horizontal fissure runs from the sternum along the fourth costal cartilage to meet the oblique fissure near the midaxillary line. This geometry explains the physical examination: the lower lobes lie mostly posterior and are heard from the back, the right middle lobe and lingula lie anterior and are heard from the front, and the upper lobes occupy the apex and upper anterior chest. On a frontal radiograph, consolidation of the right middle lobe erases the right heart border, the lingula erases the left heart border, and the lower lobes erase the hemidiaphragms, because air no longer separates tissues of similar density (the silhouette sign).
Where aspirated material goes

The right main bronchus is wider and leaves the trachea at a steeper angle, closer to the line of the trachea, so inhaled foreign bodies and aspirated secretions usually enter the right lung. Gravity then decides the segment. In an upright patient, material falls into the most dependent bronchi, the basal segments of the right lower lobe. In a supine patient the most dependent bronchi point backward: the superior segment of the right lower lobe and the posterior segment of the right upper lobe. Aspiration typically follows depressed consciousness or impaired swallowing, as with alcohol intoxication, seizures, anesthesia, or stroke.

blocks.title: Aspiration in a supine patient
steps: Cough and swallowing reflexes fail
Oral contents enter the larynx and trachea
Material follows the wider, steeper right main bronchus
Gravity carries it into backward-pointing bronchi
It lodges in the RLL superior or RUL posterior segment
Mouth flora cause pneumonia that can form an abscess
blocks.caption: Position at the time of aspiration predicts the segment involved.

blocks.predict: A man found unconscious on his back after heavy drinking develops a lung abscess. Which segment is most likely involved, and would the answer change if he had aspirated while sitting?
blocks.explain: Supine, the dependent bronchi of the right lung point posteriorly, so the superior segment of the right lower lobe (or posterior segment of the right upper lobe) is most likely. Sitting, material falls straight down into the basal segments of the right lower lobe.
blocks.check: The aspiration paragraph and flow above.

sections.title: Structures at the hilum and their arrangement

blocks.text: The root of the lung is the bundle of structures that joins the lung to the heart and trachea; the hilum is where that bundle enters the medial surface. Each root contains a main bronchus, one pulmonary artery, two pulmonary veins, bronchial arteries and veins, the pulmonary nerve plexus, and bronchopulmonary (hilar) lymph nodes. A sleeve of pleura surrounds the root, where visceral and parietal pleura are continuous, and hangs below it as the pulmonary ligament.

The pattern at each hilum follows how each pulmonary artery reaches its lung. The pulmonary trunk divides below the aortic arch. The left pulmonary artery is short and arches over the left main bronchus, so it lies superior to the bronchus. The right pulmonary artery is longer, passes under the arch and behind the ascending aorta and superior vena cava, and arrives in front of the right bronchial tree. Because the right upper lobe bronchus branches off before the artery reaches it, that bronchus lies above the artery and is called the eparterial bronchus; the rest of the right bronchial tree is hyparterial, and the right pulmonary artery lies anterior to the right main bronchus.

blocks.title: Arrangement of the hilar structures
rows: Superior to the main bronchus (highest structure)
Posterior; upper lobe (eparterial) bronchus is the highest structure
blocks.caption: Right artery anterior, left artery superior. On both sides the bronchi are posterior and the veins anterior and inferior.

blocks.text: On both sides the two pulmonary veins are the most anterior and most inferior structures of the root, because they descend to enter the left atrium below the level of the pulmonary artery bifurcation. Bronchial arteries (usually two on the left from the thoracic aorta and one on the right, often from the third right posterior intercostal artery) run on the back of the bronchi. The phrenic nerve passes in front of each root and the vagus nerve behind it, which is how a hilar tumor can involve either nerve.

Because the left pulmonary artery climbs over the left bronchus, the left hilum normally sits slightly higher than the right on a frontal radiograph; reversal of this relation suggests volume loss or a mass. Enlarged hilar lymph nodes, as in sarcoidosis (often bilateral and symmetric), tuberculosis, lymphoma, or metastatic carcinoma, widen the hilar shadow. Central lung carcinomas, especially squamous cell and small cell types, arise near the hilum and can narrow a main bronchus to cause collapse of the lung beyond it. On the left, a mass near the hilum and aortic arch can stretch the left recurrent laryngeal nerve as it loops under the arch, producing hoarseness, and involvement of the phrenic nerve in front of the root paralyzes the hemidiaphragm.

sections.title: Compartments of the mediastinum and the masses that arise in them

blocks.text: The mediastinum is the central partition of the thorax between the pleural sacs, extending from the thoracic inlet to the diaphragm and from the sternum to the vertebral bodies. A horizontal plane from the sternal angle to the T4 to T5 intervertebral disc (the transverse thoracic plane) divides it into superior and inferior parts. The same plane marks the tracheal bifurcation, the beginning and end of the aortic arch, and the entry of the azygos vein into the superior vena cava, so it is a reliable landmark. The pericardium then divides the inferior mediastinum into anterior, middle, and posterior compartments.

blocks.title: Mediastinal compartments and their contents
rows: Thoracic inlet to the T4 to T5 plane
Thymus, brachiocephalic veins, upper SVC, aortic arch and branches, trachea, esophagus, thoracic duct, vagus, phrenic, and left recurrent laryngeal nerves
Thymic remnant (thymus in children), fat, lymph nodes, sternopericardial ligaments
Heart, pericardium, ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, lower SVC, phrenic nerves, tracheobronchial lymph nodes
Pericardium and diaphragm to T5 to T12 vertebral bodies
Esophagus, descending aorta, azygos and hemiazygos veins, thoracic duct, vagus nerves, lymph nodes; sympathetic trunks lie just lateral in the paravertebral gutters
blocks.caption: The superior mediastinum is layered from front to back: thymus, veins, arteries, trachea, esophagus, thoracic duct.

blocks.text: A mediastinal mass usually comes from a tissue that belongs in its compartment, so localization on a lateral radiograph or CT narrows the diagnosis considerably. Age matters as well: in children, neurogenic tumors and lymphoma predominate; in adults, thymoma, lymphoma, and benign cysts are common.

blocks.title: Typical masses by compartment
rows: Thymoma, teratoma and other germ cell tumors, lymphoma, retrosternal thyroid
Thymus, midline germ cell rests, lymph nodes, thyroid extending from the neck
Lymph node enlargement, bronchogenic cyst, pericardial cyst
Nodes along the airways, foregut buds, pericardium
Neurogenic tumors (schwannoma, neurofibroma; neuroblastoma or ganglioneuroma in children), esophageal lesions, aortic aneurysm
Nerve roots, sympathetic ganglia, esophagus, aorta
blocks.caption: Anterior masses are often summarized as the four Ts: thymoma, teratoma, thyroid, and (terrible) lymphoma.

blocks.text: Thymoma is the classic anterior mass of adults. Many patients with thymoma have myasthenia gravis, and thymoma is also associated with pure red cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinemia. The link is immunologic: neoplastic thymic epithelium selects T cells abnormally, so autoreactive T cells escape and support autoantibody production, for example against the acetylcholine receptor. Germ cell tumors arise from germ cells that lodged along the midline during their migration and occur mainly in young men; nonseminomatous types may raise serum alpha-fetoprotein or hCG. Mediastinal lymphoma includes nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma in young adults and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma in adolescents.

Symptoms follow what the mass compresses. An anterior or superior mass can obstruct the thin-walled superior vena cava (facial and arm swelling, distended neck veins) or compress the trachea, which may worsen when the patient lies supine. A middle mass can compress a bronchus or the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. A posterior neurogenic tumor can grow through an intervertebral foramen into a dumbbell shape and compress the spinal cord, or involve the sympathetic chain.

sections.title: Innervation of the pleura and referred shoulder pain

blocks.text: The two pleural layers come from different embryonic layers and inherit different nerves. The parietal pleura develops from somatic mesoderm of the body wall, so it is supplied by somatic sensory nerves that signal sharp, well-localized pain. The visceral pleura develops from splanchnic mesoderm with the lung, so it shares the lung's autonomic supply from the pulmonary plexus, which carries stretch and reflex information but not sharp localized pain. The two layers are separated by a thin film of fluid at a pressure of about -5 cm H2O at rest, which keeps the lung expanded against the chest wall.

blocks.title: Nerve supply of the pleura
rows: Lower chest wall and upper abdominal wall
Shoulder and base of the neck
Shoulder and base of the neck
blocks.caption: Pain sensitivity follows somatic innervation, which only the parietal pleura has.

blocks.text: Pleuritic pain is sharp, localized, and worse with deep inspiration or coughing, because each breath slides and stretches the inflamed parietal layer; a pleural friction rub may be heard as the roughened surfaces move. A process confined to the lung and visceral pleura, such as an early pneumonia or a small central tumor, can therefore be painless. Pain appears once the process reaches the parietal pleura, for example when pneumonia extends to the surface or a pulmonary infarct after an embolus involves the pleura over it.
Why diaphragmatic irritation hurts in the shoulder

The phrenic nerve arises from C3, C4, and C5. Its sensory fibers from the central diaphragmatic and mediastinal pleura, and from the pericardium, enter the same cord segments as the supraclavicular nerves (C3 and C4), which supply the skin over the shoulder and clavicle. The brain has learned to attribute activity in these segments to the skin, so it refers the pain there. The irritant can come from above the diaphragm (pleurisy, pericarditis) or from below it (blood, pus, or bile against the peritoneal surface of the central diaphragm), and the pain appears on the same side as the irritated half.

blocks.title: Referred shoulder pain from the central diaphragm
steps: Inflammation, blood, or pus irritates the central diaphragm
Phrenic sensory fibers carry the signal
They synapse in cord segments C3 to C5
Supraclavicular nerves from shoulder skin enter the same segments
Convergent dorsal horn neurons project to the cortex
Pain is perceived over the shoulder
blocks.caption: Irritation of the peripheral diaphragm instead travels in lower intercostal nerves and is felt over the lower chest and upper abdomen.

blocks.text: The peripheral rim of the diaphragm and its pleura are supplied by the lower intercostal and subcostal nerves, which also supply the anterior abdominal wall. Basal pleurisy can therefore present as upper abdominal pain and guarding, and lower lobe pneumonia is a recognized mimic of an acute abdomen.

sections.title: Openings of the diaphragm and the phrenic nerve

blocks.text: The diaphragm is a dome of skeletal muscle inserting into a central tendon. Its muscle arises from the xiphoid, the lower six costal cartilages, and the lumbar vertebrae through two crura and the arcuate ligaments. Each structure that passes between thorax and abdomen crosses a different part of the diaphragm, and that part determines how the structure behaves when the muscle contracts.

blocks.title: Major openings of the diaphragm
rows: Caval opening, in the central tendon
Inferior vena cava, branches of the right phrenic nerve
Tendon is pulled taut, opening widens, venous return aided
Esophageal hiatus, in the muscle of the right crus
Esophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, esophageal branches of left gastric vessels
Crural fibers pinch the esophagus, adding to the antireflux barrier
Aortic hiatus, behind the median arcuate ligament
None; the aorta lies behind the diaphragm, not through it
blocks.caption: Smaller openings: the splanchnic nerves pierce the crura, the hemiazygos vein passes through the left crus, the sympathetic trunks pass behind the medial arcuate ligaments, and the left phrenic nerve pierces the left dome.

blocks.text: The vagal trunks follow the esophagus, so the anterior trunk (mainly from the left vagus) and posterior trunk (mainly from the right vagus) pass at T10. The thoracic duct and azygos vein run beside the aorta and pass with it at T12. Weakness or widening of the esophageal hiatus allows the stomach to herniate into the thorax (hiatal hernia), and the loss of crural support helps explain the reflux that often accompanies a sliding hernia. A posterolateral defect in the developing diaphragm, usually on the left, allows abdominal viscera into the chest and causes pulmonary hypoplasia.
The phrenic nerve

The diaphragm develops largely from the septum transversum and pleuroperitoneal membranes, which form at the level of the cervical somites and receive their nerve supply there before descending with the heart and lungs. That is why a muscle at the level of the lower ribs is supplied from the neck. Each phrenic nerve (C3 to C5, mainly C4) runs down the front of the anterior scalene, enters the thorax between the subclavian artery and vein, and passes anterior to the lung root along the pericardium. It provides all motor supply to its half of the diaphragm and sensory supply to the central diaphragm, mediastinal pleura, and pericardium; the periphery of the diaphragm receives sensory fibers from the lower intercostal and subcostal nerves.

A spinal cord injury at or above C3 removes all diaphragmatic function, so spontaneous breathing stops, whereas an injury below C5 spares the diaphragm. A unilateral phrenic lesion, from surgery, trauma, or a tumor at the hilum or neck, leaves a raised hemidiaphragm on a radiograph. On fluoroscopy during a sharp sniff, the paralyzed side moves upward (paradoxical motion), because the flaccid muscle is sucked up by the negative intrathoracic pressure generated by the other side.

blocks.predict: During a sniff test, a patient's left hemidiaphragm rises while the right descends. Which nerve is injured, and what would a chest radiograph show at rest?
blocks.explain: The left phrenic nerve. The right diaphragm contracts and lowers intrathoracic pressure, which pulls the flaccid left dome upward; at rest the left hemidiaphragm sits abnormally high.

sections.title: Course of the thoracic duct and chylothorax

blocks.text: The thoracic duct is the main lymphatic channel of the body. It drains lymph from the lower limbs, pelvis, abdomen, left thorax, left upper limb, and left side of the head and neck; the right lymphatic duct drains the remaining right upper quarter. Its intestinal lymph is chyle, because dietary long-chain fatty acids are reassembled in enterocytes into triglyceride-rich chylomicrons that are too large to enter blood capillaries and instead enter the lacteals. Flow is driven by valves, smooth muscle in the duct wall, and the pressure changes of breathing.

blocks.title: Course of the thoracic duct
steps: Lacteals and lumbar trunks drain to the cisterna chyli (about L1 to L2)
Duct enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus at T12
Ascends right of midline between the aorta and azygos vein
Lies behind the esophagus in the posterior mediastinum
Crosses to the left at about T5
Ascends left of the esophagus into the superior mediastinum and neck
Arches at about C7 and enters the left venous angle
blocks.caption: The left venous angle is the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins.

blocks.text: Because the duct changes sides, the level of injury predicts the side of the leak: damage below about T5 usually produces a right chylothorax and damage above it a left one. The duct can be torn by surgery on the esophagus, aorta, or heart, by neck dissection near the left venous angle, or by penetrating or blunt trauma, and it can be obstructed or invaded by tumor, of which lymphoma is the most common nontraumatic cause. Raised venous pressure at the venous angle, as with central venous thrombosis, can also impede drainage.

blocks.title: Chylous effusion compared with similar-looking fluids
rows: Long-standing effusion with a thick pleura
Over about 110 mg/dL (1.24 mmol/L); chylomicrons present
blocks.caption: A triglyceride under about 50 mg/dL makes chylothorax unlikely; in a fasting patient chyle may not look milky.

blocks.text: The milky color comes from light scattering by chylomicrons, so it fades when the patient is fasting or fed little fat. Because chyle carries dietary fat, fat-soluble vitamins, protein, and many T lymphocytes, a persistent leak causes malnutrition, lymphopenia, and impaired cellular immunity, while the accumulating fluid compresses the lung and causes dyspnea. The termination of the duct in the left neck also explains why abdominal cancers, especially gastric carcinoma, can metastasize to a left supraclavicular lymph node.

blocks.title: Predicting the side of a chylothorax
blocks.text: After an esophagectomy involving the lower third of the esophagus, a patient develops a milky right pleural effusion with triglyceride of 400 mg/dL. The lower thoracic duct lies behind the esophagus and to the right of the aorta, below its crossing at about T5, so a leak there drains into the right pleural cavity. By contrast, a left neck dissection that injures the duct near the left venous angle leaks into the left neck or, if the leak tracks downward, the left pleural cavity. The side of the effusion therefore points to the level of injury.

integration.text: Embryology explains most of this anatomy. The pleura inherits somatic or autonomic nerves from the mesoderm it develops from, which is why only the parietal layer hurts; the diaphragm keeps its cervical nerve after descending, which is why its central part refers pain to the shoulder; and mediastinal masses reflect resident tissues, migrating germ cells, and foregut buds. Physiology and pathology build on the same map: negative pleural pressure holds the lung to the chest wall, gravity and bronchial geometry place aspiration pneumonia and abscess (usually from mouth anaerobes), and immunology links thymoma to autoimmune disease through defective T cell selection.

These relations have limits. Surface borders vary with body habitus, respiratory phase, and posture, so clinical procedures rely on imaging rather than rib counts alone, and the paravertebral borders are approximate. Compartment lists describe typical rather than exclusive origins: lymphoma can occupy any compartment, and a mass can cross boundaries. Biochemical cutoffs for chylous fluid are guides, interpreted with the appearance, the patient's diet, and the clinical setting.

summary: At the midclavicular, midaxillary, and paravertebral lines, the lung reaches ribs 6, 8, and 10 and the pleura ribs 8, 10, and 12; the gap is the costodiaphragmatic recess, where fluid collects first.
The intercostal vein, artery, and nerve run in the costal groove under each rib, so a thoracentesis needle passes just above the rib below.
The right lung has three lobes and two fissures; the left has two lobes, one fissure, a lingula, and a cardiac notch.
The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical; aspiration goes to the right lower lobe basal segments when upright and to the superior segment of the right lower lobe when supine.
At the hilum the right pulmonary artery is anterior and the left superior to its bronchus; the veins are anterior and inferior on both sides.
The sternal angle plane (T4 to T5) divides the superior from the inferior mediastinum; anterior masses are thymoma, teratoma, lymphoma, and thyroid, and posterior masses are mainly neurogenic.
Parietal pleura is pain-sensitive through intercostal and phrenic nerves; visceral pleura has only autonomic supply.
Central diaphragmatic irritation refers pain to the shoulder because phrenic (C3 to C5) and supraclavicular (C3, C4) afferents share cord segments.
The IVC passes at T8 through the central tendon, the esophagus and vagal trunks at T10, and the aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein at T12; the phrenic nerve is the sole motor supply.
The thoracic duct runs from the cisterna chyli through the aortic hiatus, crosses left at about T5, and ends at the left venous angle; its injury causes a triglyceride-rich chylothorax.

verify: Thoracentesis site: Moore describes the ninth intercostal space at the midaxillary line during expiration; current clinical practice uses imaging-guided sites. Confirm which wording NABNE expects.
The lower border numbers (lung 6, 8, 10; pleura 8, 10, 12) are the conventional teaching values; some texts give the paravertebral lung border as about T10 spinous process rather than rib 10.

The fluid volume needed to blunt the costophrenic angle on an upright radiograph (often quoted as about 200 mL on a frontal view and less on a lateral view) varies between sources and was not stated here.
Bronchial artery origins (two left from the aorta, one right often from the third right posterior intercostal artery) vary considerably among individuals.
The proportion of thymoma patients with myasthenia gravis is quoted from about 30% to 50% in different sources, so no figure is stated.
Chylothorax cutoffs (triglyceride over about 110 mg/dL, under about 50 mg/dL unlikely, cholesterol under about 200 mg/dL) follow common consensus values; confirm the values NABNE uses.
The rule that thoracic duct injury below about T5 gives a right chylothorax and above it a left one is a classic teaching generalization; confirm NABNE emphasis.
The mnemonic of the four Ts for anterior mediastinal masses is widely used; confirm it is acceptable in NABNE-aligned materials.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: thorax-surface-lines (lung and pleural borders at three lines), intercostal-space (neurovascular bundle and needle path), lung-hila (right and left hilar arrangement), mediastinum-compartments (sagittal view with superior, anterior, middle, posterior), diaphragm-openings (inferior view with T8, T10, T12).
